title: Why is there suffering?
hook: Christians have wrestled with this for millennia and offered no easy answer

segments.voice: Yesterday closed a block on rites, rooms and arts: the house of prayer. Your line was faith has a body. Where did you notice yours? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-seven.

"O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" That isn't a skeptic in a debate hall. It's a prophet, Habakkuk, in the opening lines of his book, watching violence and injustice go on and on while heaven seems quiet. The same question turns up at hospital bedsides, in the late news, at a funeral for someone who died far too young. If God is good, and God is strong, why this? A new block begins today, on suffering, doubt and the hardest questions. It starts with the hardest one. Today: why is there suffering?

Today's word is theodicy. It's the name philosophers and theologians give to any attempt to show that God is good in a world full of pain. Put the problem in three short lines. God is good. God is powerful. Terrible things happen. Something seems to have to give. The Bible doesn't hide from it. In Luke's Gospel, people bring Jesus news of Galileans killed by Pilate, and Jesus raises a second disaster himself: a tower in Siloam fell and killed eighteen people. He asks, in the King James Bible: "think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?" And he answers: no. In John's Gospel, his disciples pass a man born blind and ask, "Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?" Jesus says, "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents." Twice, he refuses the neat equation: you suffer, so you must have done something. Christians have offered answers anyway. Some say God gave people real freedom, and freedom can be used to wound. Some say suffering can refine a person, the way fire tests gold, a picture Peter's first letter uses for faith. Some point to the end of the story, in Revelation: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain." And some, after all the arguments, say the honest thing: we don't know. Some who have sat with deep suffering add a warning. An answer that sounds wise in a classroom can sound cheap at a bedside. That's today's line: no easy answers. Not no answers. Christians do say God is good, and that God is with those who suffer. The days ahead hold that beside the question, not on top of it.
screen: `FREEDOM, FIRE, THE END OF THE STORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with the question honestly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one piece of suffering you can't make sense of. Your own, or someone else's, or something far away. Don't solve it. Don't argue it away. Just hold it, the way you'd hold someone's hand. When a quick answer pops up, notice it, and set it down. If you pray, you can bring the question to God the way Habakkuk did: how long. If you don't, let the question simply be asked, into the quiet, and leave it open. The bell holds the time.
Theodicy. Any attempt to show that God is good when the world is full of suffering.
Your line: no easy answers. Today, if someone tells you about something hard, skip the quick explanation, and just say: that's hard. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Christians bring the question of suffering to prayer, to Scripture, especially Job, the Psalms and the cross, and to pastors and friends; churches hold different explanations side by side, and some sit with the question rather than settle it.

trapdoor: what you thought: theodicy is a puzzle for a philosophy class.
what it means: the attempt to hold God's goodness and the world's pain together, honestly, without easy answers.
what a scholar hears: Luke 13 and John 9, where Jesus twice refuses to say that the people who suffered had it coming.
